topic.title: Recursion & Backtracking
topic.summary: Think recursively: base case, call stack and the choose → explore → un-choose template behind subsets, permutations, combinations, valid parentheses, N-Queens and word search.
topic.overview:
**Recursion** is a function solving a problem by calling itself on a smaller input. **Backtracking** is recursion that builds a candidate one decision at a time and **undoes** each decision when it leads nowhere. Together they answer every "generate all …" question (subsets, permutations, combinations, valid parentheses) and constraint puzzles such as N-Queens, Sudoku and word search.

### What interviewers expect from a new grad
- Explain the **base case**, the recursive case and what the **call stack** holds; know that recursion depth costs O(depth) space and can overflow.
- Write the backtracking template from memory: **choose → explore → un-choose**.
- Pick the right variant: a **start index** (subsets, combinations), a **used[]** array (permutations), **row by row with constraint sets** (N-Queens), **grid DFS with mark / unmark** (word search).
- State the size of the output — 2ⁿ, n!, a Catalan number, 4ᵏ — because it *is* the time complexity, and explain how **pruning** cuts the tree.
- Draw the recursion tree when stuck. Interviewers like candidates who visualise the search.

### How to study this topic
1. Trace `factorial` and `myPow` by hand until the call stack feels concrete.
2. Code **Subsets** and **Permutations** until the template is automatic, and compare their loops.
3. Add constraints: **Combination Sum** (target + reuse), **Generate Parentheses** (validity rules), **Letter Combinations** (one level per digit).
4. Finish with the board problems: **Word Search** and **N-Queens**.
5. For every problem say the brute force, the tree size and the pruning rule out loud.

cheatsheet.title: Recursion essentials
points: Base case first: the smallest input you can answer directly
The recursive case must shrink the input toward the base case
Each call has its own stack frame → depth d costs O(d) space
No tail-call optimisation in V8/Node, CPython or the JVM; Python's default limit is 1000 frames
Two calls on n/2 per level is O(n); one call reused is O(log n) — count the nodes of the tree

cheatsheet.title: Backtracking template
points: choose: change the shared state (push, mark used, place a queen)
explore: recurse to the next decision
un-choose: undo exactly what you changed, in reverse order
Record a copy of the path, never the shared reference
Recurse with i + 1 (each item once), with i (reuse allowed), or loop from 0 with used[] (order matters)

cheatsheet.title: Output size = time complexity
points: Subsets: 2ⁿ (× n to copy each)
Permutations: n! (× n)
Combinations of size k: C(n, k)
Valid parentheses: Catalan(n) ≈ 4ⁿ / (n^1.5·√π)
Phone letter combinations: up to 4ᵏ
Word search on a grid: O(R·C·3^L)

cheatsheet.title: Pruning tricks
points: Sort, then break as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target
Skip equal neighbours at the same level to avoid duplicate answers (sort first)
Keep constraint sets (columns, diagonals, used cells) for O(1) checks
Return true up the stack as soon as one answer is enough
Reject impossible inputs up front (letter counts, sums that are too small)

cheatsheet.title: Language notes
points: JavaScript: RangeError "Maximum call stack size exceeded"; copy with [...path]
Python: RecursionError; copy with path[:]; sys.setrecursionlimit raises the limit but too high can crash the interpreter
Java: StackOverflowError; copy with new ArrayList<>(path); undo with path.remove(path.size() - 1)

questions.title: Recursion Basics: power(x, n) and the Call Stack
questions.prompt:
Implement `myPow(x, n)` that returns **x raised to the power n** using recursion and without calling a built-in power function.

- `x` is a floating-point number and `n` is a 32-bit signed integer, so `n` can be **negative** (x⁻ⁿ = 1 / xⁿ) or **zero** (x⁰ = 1).
- Multiplying `x` by itself n times is too slow for n ≈ 2³¹: aim for **O(log n)** multiplications.

Interviewers use this problem to check that you can explain the **base case**, what happens on the **call stack** for each call, and why the recursion terminates.
constraints: The answer fits in a double
hints: What is the smallest n whose answer you know without any work? That is your base case.
x¹⁰ = x⁵ · x⁵. If you already know x⁵, how many more multiplications do you need?
Compute half = myPow(x, ⌊n/2⌋) once, then return half·half for even n and half·half·x for odd n. Turn a negative n into 1 / myPow(x, -n).

approaches.name: Naive recursion
approaches.idea: myPow(x, n) = x · myPow(x, n - 1) with base case n = 0. One stack frame per decrement, so n = 10⁶ overflows the call stack.

approaches.name: Iterative loop
approaches.idea: Multiply x into a result |n| times. No stack risk, but still linear and far too slow for n ≈ 2³¹.

approaches.name: Fast power (halving)
approaches.idea: Recurse once on ⌊n/2⌋, square the result and multiply one extra x when n is odd.

solution.summary: Divide and conquer: xⁿ = (x^(n/2))² for even n and (x^(n/2))²·x for odd n. I recurse on n/2 once per level, stop at the base case n = 0 (return 1), and turn a negative n into 1 / x^(-n). That is O(log n) time and O(log n) stack depth.
solution.explanation:
**Recursion** means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a *smaller* input. Every correct recursive function has two parts:

1. **Base case** — an input small enough to answer directly (here `n === 0` → `1`). Without a reachable base case the calls never stop and the program crashes with a stack overflow (`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in JavaScript, `RecursionError` in Python, `StackOverflowError` in Java).
2. **Recursive case** — shrink the input toward the base case (here `n → ⌊n/2⌋`) and combine the smaller answer into the bigger one.

Then take the **leap of faith**: assume `myPow(x, ⌊n/2⌋)` is correct and only think about how to use its result.

### What the call stack does
Every call gets its own **stack frame** holding its parameters and locals (`x`, `n`, `half`). A frame that makes a recursive call **waits** until that call returns. For `myPow(2, 10)` the frames n = 10, 5, 2, 1, 0 are pushed; the base case returns 1 and the results flow back as frames pop: 1 → 2 → 4 → 32 → 1024. The deepest stack size is the recursion's **extra space**.

The classic warm-up uses the same structure:
```js
function factorial(n) {
  if (n <= 1) return 1;        // base case
  return n * factorial(n - 1); // recursive case: n frames deep
}
```

### Why halving is fast
Because n halves on every call, there are only about log₂ n + 1 levels: n = 2³¹ needs ~32 calls instead of two billion multiplications. Odd n loses one factor when floored, so it is multiplied back in (`half * half * x`).

### Edge cases
- `n = 0` → 1.
- Negative `n` → `1 / myPow(x, -n)`.
- Java: `-n` overflows for `n = -2³¹` (`Integer.MIN_VALUE`), so widen to `long` first.
- Call the recursion **once** and store it in `half`. `myPow(x, n/2) * myPow(x, n/2)` doubles the calls per level and silently becomes O(n).

Node (V8), CPython and the JVM do **not** perform tail-call optimisation, so deep linear recursion (thousands of frames) can overflow; Python's default recursion limit is 1000. Prefer a loop when depth grows with n.

code.code:
function myPow(x, n) {
  if (n < 0) return 1 / myPow(x, -n); // x^-n = 1 / x^n
  if (n === 0) return 1; // base case: stops the recursion
  const half = myPow(x, Math.floor(n / 2)); // ONE call on half the exponent
  if (n % 2 === 0) return half * half; // even: x^n = half * half
  return half * half * x; // odd: one extra factor of x
}

complexity.time: O(log n) — the exponent halves on every call, so there are about log₂|n| + 1 calls
complexity.space: O(log n) — one stack frame per level of recursion

keyPoints: Name the two parts of every recursive function: a base case and a recursive case that shrinks the input
Each call has its own stack frame; results flow back as frames pop in reverse order
Recurse once and reuse half: calling it twice per level is O(n)
Negative exponent → 1 / x^(-n); in Java widen to long because -(-2³¹) overflows an int
Recursion depth is extra space and can overflow the stack — mention the iterative version

visuals.title: The call stack for myPow(2, 10)
visuals.caption: Each call pushes a frame with its own n. Frames wait for the call above them, then pop in reverse order as results flow back down.

steps.note: `myPow(2, 10)` is called: a **stack frame** with its own `x = 2`, `n = 10` is pushed. n is not 0, so it must first compute `half = myPow(2, 5)` and **waits**.
`myPow(2, 5)` starts with its own `n = 5`. Not the base case, so it calls `myPow(2, 2)` and waits. Every waiting frame stays on the stack.
`myPow(2, 2)` starts with its own `n = 2`. Not the base case, so it calls `myPow(2, 1)` and waits. Every waiting frame stays on the stack.
`myPow(2, 1)` starts with its own `n = 1`. Not the base case, so it calls `myPow(2, 0)` and waits. Every waiting frame stays on the stack.
**Base case.** `n === 0`, so `myPow(2, 0)` returns 1 without calling anything. The stack is 5 frames deep — the deepest point of the recursion.
Frame n = 1 resumes with `half = 1`; n = 1 is odd → `half * half * x` = 1·1·2 = 2. The frame is popped and the value flows back to `myPow(2, 2)`, which resumes.
Frame n = 2 resumes with `half = 2`; n = 2 is even → `half * half` = 2·2 = 4. The frame is popped and the value flows back to `myPow(2, 5)`, which resumes.
Frame n = 5 resumes with `half = 4`; n = 5 is odd → `half * half * x` = 4·4·2 = 32. The frame is popped and the value flows back to `myPow(2, 10)`, which resumes.

Frame n = 10 resumes with `half = 32`; n = 10 is even → `half * half` = 32·32 = 1024. The stack is empty again: the answer is **1024** after only 5 calls (n = 10, 5, 2, 1, 0) instead of the 11 calls the naive `x * myPow(x, n - 1)` would make.

visuals.title: Recursion tree: two recursive calls vs one
visuals.caption: Each node is one call. Calling myPow(x, n/2) twice doubles the work per level; reusing half keeps one path (green).

steps.note: A tempting but slow version writes `return myPow(x, n / 2) * myPow(x, n / 2)` (n even). The root call for n = 4 makes **two** recursive calls.
Each of those again calls itself twice. The input halves at every level, but the number of calls **doubles**.
Level 2: four calls with n = 1, all computing exactly the same value.

The base cases: 15 calls in total for n = 4. There are log₂ n + 2 levels (n, n/2, …, 1, 0) and the calls double at each, so 2^(log₂ n + 2) − 1 = 4n − 1 calls — **O(n)**, no better than multiplying n times.
Storing the result in `half` and reusing it means only **one** child per level is ever computed: 4 calls (log₂ 4 + 2). That is the O(log n) solution.

pitfalls: Missing or unreachable base case → infinite recursion and a stack overflow
Calling myPow(x, n / 2) twice instead of storing it — correct but O(n)
In JavaScript n / 2 is fractional: use Math.floor (Python //, Java integer division)
Forgetting negative exponents, or negating Integer.MIN_VALUE in Java without widening to long

followUps.question: Can you do it without recursion, in O(1) extra space?
followUps.answer: Yes, binary exponentiation: result = 1; while n > 0: if n is odd, result *= x; x *= x; n >>= 1. It reads the bits of n from least to most significant.

followUps.question: How would you compute xⁿ mod m for a huge n?
followUps.answer: Same fast-power loop, taking % m after every multiplication (modular exponentiation). It is used in RSA, hashing and many "answer modulo 10⁹ + 7" problems; use long (Java) or BigInt (JS) so the product does not overflow.

followUps.question: What is tail recursion, and would it help here?
followUps.answer: A call is a tail call when nothing is left to do after it returns, so a compiler could reuse the frame. V8, CPython and the JVM do not do this, so in these languages it saves no stack; convert to a loop instead.

questions.title: Subsets (Power Set)
questions.prompt:
You are given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers. Return **every subset** of it (the *power set*), including the empty subset and the whole array.

Each subset must appear exactly once. The order of the subsets, and of the numbers inside a subset, does not matter.
hints: How many subsets does an n-element array have? Each element is either in or out.
Build a subset one element at a time. After picking nums[i], only consider elements to its right so [2,1] is never produced after [1,2].
backtrack(start): record a copy of path, then for i from start to n - 1: push nums[i], backtrack(i + 1), pop.

approaches.name: Iterative doubling
approaches.idea: Start with [[]]. For each number, copy every subset built so far and append the number to the copy.

approaches.name: Bitmask enumeration
approaches.idea: Every mask from 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 is one subset: bit i set means nums[i] is included.

approaches.name: Backtracking with a start index
approaches.idea: DFS in which every node is a subset: record path, extend it with each later element, recurse, undo.

solution.summary: Backtracking: keep a path, and in backtrack(start) first record a copy of path (every node of the recursion tree is a valid subset), then for each i ≥ start push nums[i], recurse with i + 1 and pop. There are 2ⁿ subsets and copying each costs up to n, so it is O(n·2ⁿ).
solution.explanation:
**Why 2ⁿ:** every element is independently *in* or *out*, so n elements give 2 × 2 × … × 2 = 2ⁿ subsets. Any correct algorithm must output all of them, so exponential time is expected — the constraint n ≤ 10 is the hint.

### The backtracking template: choose → explore → un-choose
1. `result` collects the answers; `path` is the subset currently being built.
2. `backtrack(start)` first pushes a **copy** of `path` into `result` — every node is an answer.
3. For each `i` from `start` to the end: **choose** `path.push(nums[i])`, **explore** `backtrack(i + 1)`, **un-choose** `path.pop()`.

**Why there are no duplicates:** `start` only moves forward, so elements are always added in index order. `[1,2]` is produced, `[2,1]` cannot be.

**Why copy:** `path` keeps changing. Pushing the same array object would leave every entry of `result` pointing to one array, which is empty at the end.

**Why undo:** all calls share one `path`. Popping after the recursive call restores exactly the state the loop had before, so the next iteration starts clean.

### Variants
- **Subsets II** (input has duplicates): sort, then skip `nums[i]` when `i > start && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]`.
- **Bitmask version:** `for mask in 0..2ⁿ-1`, include `nums[i]` when `(mask >> i) & 1` — the same 2ⁿ leaves as the include/exclude tree.

complexity.time: O(n·2ⁿ) — 2ⁿ subsets, each copied in up to O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) — recursion depth and path (the output itself holds n·2ⁿ numbers)

keyPoints: 2ⁿ subsets because each element is in or out
Choose → explore → un-choose is the backtracking template
The start index generates each subset once, in index order
Record a copy of path, never the shared reference
Mention the bitmask alternative and the Subsets II skip rule for duplicates

visuals.title: Backtracking tree for subsets([1, 2, 3])
visuals.caption: Each node is one call to backtrack and the subset it records. Blue = running call, light blue = waiting callers, green = finished.

steps.note: Call `backtrack(0)` with an empty `path`. Every node of this tree is a subset, so the call first records a copy: `[]`.
Choose 1 (`path.push`), call `backtrack(1)` and record [1].
Choose 2 (`path.push`), call `backtrack(2)` and record [1,2].
Choose 3 (`path.push`), call `backtrack(3)` and record [1,2,3]. No elements remain to its right, so its loop is empty and it returns.
Back from the recursion: pop 3, then 2 (un-choose). Choose 3 (`path.push`), call `backtrack(3)` and record [1,3]. No elements remain to its right, so its loop is empty and it returns.
Back from the recursion: pop 3, then 1 (un-choose). Choose 2 (`path.push`), call `backtrack(2)` and record [2].
Choose 3 (`path.push`), call `backtrack(3)` and record [2,3]. No elements remain to its right, so its loop is empty and it returns.
Back from the recursion: pop 3, then 2 (un-choose). Choose 3 (`path.push`), call `backtrack(3)` and record [3]. No elements remain to its right, so its loop is empty and it returns.
Done: 8 = 2³ subsets, exactly one per node. Children only add elements to the right of the last one chosen, so [2,1] can never appear after [1,2] — no duplicates.

visuals.title: Include / exclude view: why there are 2ⁿ subsets
visuals.caption: Left child = include the element, right child = skip it. The leaves are the subsets; a bitmask loop enumerates the same leaves.

steps.note: Another way to see the same answer: walk through the elements and make a **yes/no decision** for each one. Nothing is decided yet.
Decide on 1: the left branch takes it, the right branch skips it. 2 partial subsets now.
Decide on 2: the left branch takes it, the right branch skips it. 4 partial subsets now.
Decide on 3. After all 3 decisions there are 2 × 2 × 2 = **8 leaves** — exactly the 8 subsets. This is why the answer always has 2ⁿ subsets.

pitfalls: Pushing path itself instead of a copy — every result ends up as the same (empty) array
Looping from 0 instead of start — produces [2,1] as well as [1,2]
Forgetting to pop after the recursive call, so elements leak into sibling branches
Recording only at the leaves of the start-index tree and missing the shorter subsets

followUps.question: What if nums contains duplicates?
followUps.answer: Sort first, then in the loop skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]. The first copy of a value at each level is explored; identical siblings are skipped.

followUps.question: Can you do it without recursion?
followUps.answer: Yes: iterate mask from 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 and include nums[i] when bit i of mask is set, or start from [[]] and for each number append it to copies of all existing subsets.

followUps.question: How would you return only subsets of size k?
followUps.answer: Same template, but record only when path.length === k and stop recursing there (that is the Combinations problem, C(n, k) results).

questions.title: Permutations
questions.prompt:
Given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers, return **all possible orderings** (permutations) of its elements.

Every permutation uses each element exactly once. You may return them in any order.
hints: How many choices do you have for the first position? For the second? Multiply them.
Unlike subsets, order matters: at every level you may pick ANY element that is not already in the path, not just later ones.
Keep a boolean used[]. If path.length === n record a copy; otherwise for every i with !used[i]: mark, push, recurse, pop, unmark.

approaches.name: Insert into every gap
approaches.idea: Build permutations of the first k numbers, then insert number k + 1 into every position of each one. Works, but allocates many intermediate arrays.

approaches.name: Backtracking with used[]
approaches.idea: Fill positions left to right; at each level try every unused element, recurse, then undo.

approaches.name: Backtracking by swapping
approaches.idea: Swap nums[start] with each nums[i] (i ≥ start), recurse on start + 1, swap back. No used[] array, but the output order is less intuitive.

solution.summary: Backtracking over positions: at each level try every element not used yet — mark it, append it, recurse, then remove and unmark it. When the path has n elements I record a copy. There are n! permutations, each copied in O(n), so the time is O(n·n!).
solution.explanation:
**Counting first:** n choices for the first slot, n - 1 for the second, … → n! permutations. For n = 6 that is 720, which is why the constraints are tiny and an exponential answer is expected.

### Algorithm
1. `path` holds the permutation being built; `used[i]` says whether `nums[i]` is already in it.
2. **Base case:** `path.length === n` → push a **copy** of path and return.
3. Otherwise, for every index `i`: skip it if `used[i]`; else **choose** (`used[i] = true`, `path.push(nums[i])`), **explore** (`backtrack()`), **un-choose** (`path.pop()`, `used[i] = false`).

### Subsets vs permutations
Subsets loop from `start` because order does not matter. Permutations loop from **0** every time and rely on `used[]` because `[2,1]` and `[1,2]` are different answers.

### Why the undo step matters
`path` and `used` are shared by every call. Undoing after the recursive call restores exactly the state the caller had, so its next loop iteration explores a fresh branch.

### Duplicates (Permutations II)
Sort the input and skip `nums[i]` when `nums[i] === nums[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]`. That forces equal values to be used in their original order, so each distinct permutation is produced once.

code.code:
def permute(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    result, path = [], []
    used = [False] * len(nums)

    def backtrack() -> None:
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])  # complete permutation: record a copy
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i]:
                continue  # already placed earlier in path
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])  # choose
            backtrack()  # explore
            path.pop()  # un-choose
            used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return result

complexity.time: O(n·n!) — n! permutations, each copied in O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) — recursion depth, path and used[] (the output is n·n! numbers)

keyPoints: n! results, so exponential time is unavoidable — say it before coding
Loop over all indices and skip used ones (order matters, unlike subsets)
Choose → explore → un-choose; undo both path and used[]
Record a copy when path.length == n
Know the duplicate rule: sort and skip nums[i] == nums[i-1] when !used[i-1]

visuals.title: Backtracking with used[] on nums = [1, 2, 3]
visuals.caption: Blue = just chosen, light blue = already in path, green = a complete permutation. The first branch is shown one choice at a time.

steps.note: Start with an empty `path` and `used = [F, F, F]`. Position 0 of the permutation can be **any** of the 3 numbers.
Choose nums[0] = 1: set `used[0] = true` and push it. Then recurse to fill the next position.
Choose nums[1] = 2: set `used[1] = true` and push it. The loop skipped index 0 because it is already used.
Choose 3. `path.length === 3` → record **[1,2,3]**.
Undo 3, then 2 (pop + unmark). Choose 3, then 2. `path.length === 3` → record **[1,3,2]**.
Undo 2, then 3, then 1 (pop + unmark). Choose 2, then 1, then 3. `path.length === 3` → record **[2,1,3]**.
Undo 3, then 1 (pop + unmark). Choose 3, then 1. `path.length === 3` → record **[2,3,1]**.
Undo 1, then 3, then 2 (pop + unmark). Choose 3, then 1, then 2. `path.length === 3` → record **[3,1,2]**.
Undo 2, then 1 (pop + unmark). Choose 2, then 1. `path.length === 3` → record **[3,2,1]**.
All 6 = 3! permutations recorded. `used` is all F again: every choice was undone on the way back.

visuals.title: Decision tree: 3 × 2 × 1 choices
visuals.caption: Nodes are calls that still have a choice to make. The final, forced choice completes a permutation (shown in the result panel).

steps.note: The first position can hold any of **3** numbers.
Each branch has **2** unused numbers left for the second position (`used[]` skips the one already taken).
After two choices exactly **1** number is left, so 3 × 2 = 6 branches remain.
The forced last choice completes each branch: 3 × 2 × 1 = **3! = 6** permutations. For n numbers the tree has n! leaves, so the work is O(n·n!).

visuals.title: Subsets vs combinations vs permutations: the three backtracking templates
rows: Sort, skip nums[i] == nums[i-1] when i > start
Sort, skip when nums[i] == nums[i-1] and !used[i-1]

pitfalls: Starting the loop at a start index (subsets template) — you get combinations, not permutations
Forgetting to reset used[i] = false after the recursive call
Recording path itself instead of a copy
Using indexOf/includes on path to test usage — works for distinct values but costs O(n) per check and breaks with duplicates

followUps.question: What if nums has duplicates?
followUps.answer: Sort it and skip nums[i] when nums[i] == nums[i-1] and used[i-1] is false. Equal values are then always placed in a fixed order, so duplicates are never generated.

followUps.question: How do you find only the next permutation in lexicographic order?
followUps.answer: Use the O(n) next-permutation algorithm: find the rightmost i with a[i] < a[i+1], swap a[i] with the rightmost element larger than it, then reverse the suffix after i.

followUps.question: How would you return the k-th permutation without generating all of them?
followUps.answer: Use the factorial number system: the first element is index ⌊(k-1)/(n-1)!⌋ of the remaining numbers; repeat with the remainder. O(n²) with a list, no backtracking.

questions.title: Combination Sum
questions.prompt:
You are given an array of **distinct** positive integers `candidates` and a positive integer `target`. Return every **unique combination** of candidates whose numbers add up to `target`.

- A candidate may be used **any number of times** in a combination.
- Two combinations are the same if they contain the same numbers with the same counts, so `[2,2,3]` and `[3,2,2]` count once.
- Return the combinations in any order.

examples.explanation: Any sum of 4s and 6s is even

constraints: The answer has fewer than 150 combinations
hints: This is like subsets, except you may take the same number again and you stop when the sum reaches target.
To avoid [2,3,2] and [2,2,3] both appearing, only pick candidates at an index ≥ the last one you picked.
backtrack(start, remaining): if remaining is 0 record; for i ≥ start push nums[i] and recurse with (i, remaining - nums[i]) — i, not i + 1. Sort first so you can break when nums[i] > remaining.

approaches.name: Generate and filter
approaches.idea: Enumerate every multiset of candidates of length up to target / min(candidates) and keep those that sum to target. Explores huge numbers of useless combinations.

approaches.name: Backtracking, no pruning
approaches.idea: Recurse with remaining - nums[i] and return when remaining < 0.
approaches.time: O(N^(T/M)) — N candidates, depth ≤ target / smallest

approaches.name: Sorted backtracking with break
approaches.idea: Sort once; break the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds remaining, cutting off all larger candidates at once.
approaches.time: Same worst case, far fewer calls in practice

solution.summary: Backtracking with a start index and a running remainder: try candidates[i] for i ≥ start, recurse with (i, remaining - candidates[i]) so the same number can be reused, record when remaining hits 0, and — after sorting — break as soon as a candidate is larger than what remains.
solution.explanation:
Think of it as "subsets with repetition that must hit an exact sum".

1. Sort the candidates.
2. `backtrack(start, remaining)`: if `remaining === 0`, push a copy of `path`.
3. Otherwise loop `i` from `start`: if `nums[i] > remaining`, **break** (sorted, so every later candidate is too big as well); else push `nums[i]`, recurse with `(i, remaining - nums[i])`, pop.

**Why pass `i`, not `i + 1`?** Passing `i` lets the same candidate be chosen again (`[2,2,3]`). Passing `i + 1` means each number at most once — that is Combination Sum II.

**Why the start index removes duplicates:** numbers are always added in non-decreasing index order, so `[2,2,3]` is generated but `[2,3,2]` and `[3,2,2]` are never explored.

**Why sorting helps:** without sorting you can only `continue` past a too-large candidate; with sorting one comparison prunes the rest of the loop. In the tree for `[2,3,5]`, target 7, only 10 calls are made.

**Complexity:** with N candidates, target T and smallest candidate M, the tree is at most T/M deep with branching ≤ N, so O(N^(T/M)) calls in the worst case (plus copying each answer). It is exponential, but the constraints keep it small.

complexity.time: O(N^(T/M)) — branching ≤ N, depth ≤ target / smallest candidate; pruning cuts most branches
complexity.space: O(T/M) — recursion depth and path (output excluded)

keyPoints: Same template as subsets, but record only when remaining == 0
Recurse with i (not i + 1) to allow reuse
The start index prevents permutations of the same combination
Sort, then break (not continue) when a candidate exceeds remaining
Explain the exponential bound with depth T/M and branching N

steps.note: Sorted candidates = [2,3,5]. Call `backtrack(0, 7)`: we need 7 more and may start from index 0.
Choose 2: path [2], call `backtrack(0, 5)`. 5 is still positive, so keep going. `start` stays 0, which lets 2 be chosen again.
Choose 2: path [2,2], call `backtrack(0, 3)`. 3 is still positive, so keep going. `start` stays 0, which lets 2 be chosen again.
Choose 2: path [2,2,2], call `backtrack(0, 1)`. The smallest allowed candidate 2 is already > 1, so the loop **breaks** at once. Dead end — return.
Choose 3: path [2,2,3], call `backtrack(1, 0)`. Remaining is **0** → record [2,2,3].

Back at [2,2] (remaining 3): next candidate 5 > 3 → break. Choose 3: path [2,3], call `backtrack(1, 2)`. The smallest allowed candidate 3 is already > 2, so the loop **breaks** at once. Dead end — return.
Choose 5: path [2,5], call `backtrack(2, 0)`. Remaining is **0** → record [2,5].
Choose 3: path [3], call `backtrack(1, 4)`. 4 is still positive, so keep going. `start` stays 1, which lets 3 be chosen again.
Choose 3: path [3,3], call `backtrack(1, 1)`. The smallest allowed candidate 3 is already > 1, so the loop **breaks** at once. Dead end — return.

Back at [3] (remaining 4): next candidate 5 > 4 → break. Choose 5: path [5], call `backtrack(2, 2)`. The smallest allowed candidate 5 is already > 2, so the loop **breaks** at once. Dead end — return.
Search finished: 2 combinations. Sorting + `break` pruned every branch whose next candidate was too big, so only 10 calls were made.

start index + skip c[i] == c[i-1] when i > start
Same, plus stop when path.length == k

pitfalls: Recursing with i + 1 — loses combinations that reuse a number
Looping from 0 instead of start — returns [2,2,3], [2,3,2] and [3,2,2]
Using break without sorting first — skips valid larger-index candidates
Forgetting to pop after the recursive call

followUps.question: What if each candidate can be used only once and the input has duplicates?
followUps.answer: Combination Sum II: sort, recurse with i + 1, and skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1] so equal values do not start duplicate branches at the same level.

followUps.question: What if you only need the number of combinations, not the lists?
followUps.answer: Use dynamic programming like the coin-change-ways problem: ways[0] = 1; for each coin, for s from coin to target, ways[s] += ways[s - coin]. O(N·T) time.

questions.title: Generate Parentheses
questions.prompt:
Given an integer `n`, return **every well-formed string** that uses exactly `n` pairs of parentheses.

A string is well-formed when every `(` has a matching `)` after it and no `)` appears before its `(` — for example `(())` and `()()` are valid, `())(` is not. Any order is accepted.
hints: You could generate all 2^(2n) strings and validate each. Can you avoid ever building an invalid prefix?
Track how many ( and ) you have used so far. When is adding ( legal? When is adding ) legal?
Add ( while open < n; add ) only while close < open. When the length reaches 2n the string is valid — record it.

approaches.name: Generate all, then validate
approaches.idea: Build all 2^(2n) strings of ( and ) and keep those that pass a balance check.

approaches.name: Backtracking with open/close counts
approaches.idea: Only add ( while open < n and ) while close < open, so every prefix stays valid and every leaf is an answer.
approaches.time: O(4ⁿ / √n) — proportional to the Catalan number of results × n

solution.summary: Backtracking with two counters: I may add "(" while open < n and ")" only while close < open. Those rules keep every prefix valid, so when the length reaches 2n the string is a correct answer. The number of results is the n-th Catalan number, roughly 4ⁿ / (n·√n).
solution.explanation:
**Key insight:** a prefix can still become a valid string exactly when `close ≤ open ≤ n`. So instead of generating everything and filtering, enforce that invariant on every step.

1. `backtrack(open, close)` with the current `path`.
2. If `path.length === 2n` → record it (it is valid by construction).
3. If `open < n` → add `(`, recurse with `open + 1`, remove it.
4. If `close < open` → add `)`, recurse with `close + 1`, remove it.

**Why it is correct:** rule 3 never uses more than n opening brackets; rule 4 never closes a bracket that is not open, so the balance never goes negative. At length 2n we have open = close = n, which is exactly a balanced string. Every valid string is reachable because each of its prefixes satisfies both rules.

**How many answers?** The n-th **Catalan number** C(n) = (2n)! / ((n + 1)!·n!): 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, … It grows like 4ⁿ / (n^1.5·√π), and each answer costs O(n) to build, which is the time complexity.

**Interview tip:** say the brute force first (2^(2n) strings), then explain how the two rules prune it — that is the "backtracking = brute force + pruning" idea interviewers want to hear.

code.code:
def generate_parenthesis(n: int) -> list[str]:
    result, path = [], []

    def backtrack(open_: int, close: int) -> None:
        if len(path) == 2 * n:
            result.append(''.join(path))  # complete and valid
            return
        if open_ < n:  # an opening bracket is still available
            path.append('(')
            backtrack(open_ + 1, close)
            path.pop()
        if close < open_:  # only close a bracket that is open
            path.append(')')
            backtrack(open_, close + 1)
            path.pop()

    backtrack(0, 0)
    return result

complexity.time: O(4ⁿ / √n) — Catalan(n) = Θ(4ⁿ / n^1.5) answers, each built in O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) — recursion depth and path are at most 2n

keyPoints: State the brute force (2^(2n) strings + validation), then prune
Two rules: add ( while open < n, add ) while close < open
Every leaf is valid by construction — no final check
Count of answers is the Catalan number
Mention it is the same choose → explore → un-choose template

Add ')' → "(()" (open = 2, close = 1). open = n = 2: every '(' is used, so adding '(' is **rejected** (red). Only ')' can follow.
Add ')' → "(())" (open = 2, close = 2). Length 4 reached → record **(())**. It is valid by construction, no check needed.
Add ')' → "()" (open = 1, close = 1). open < n, so '(' is allowed — try it first.

pitfalls: Allowing ) whenever close < n instead of close < open — produces strings like ")("

Mixing the two string styles: passing s + "(" creates a new string, so there is nothing to undo; appending to a shared array or StringBuilder needs a pop after every call — doing both, or neither, corrupts the results
Validating each finished string again — unnecessary work
Forgetting to pop after the recursive call when using a shared array or StringBuilder

followUps.question: How would you check whether a given string of brackets is valid?
followUps.answer: Scan once with a balance counter (+1 for (, -1 for )); fail if it goes negative, succeed if it ends at 0. With several bracket types, use a stack.

followUps.question: How many valid strings are there for n = 10?
followUps.answer: Catalan(10) = 16,796. The formula is C(n) = (2n)! / ((n + 1)!·n!).

questions.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
questions.prompt:
On an old phone keypad each digit from 2 to 9 maps to letters: 2 → abc, 3 → def, 4 → ghi, 5 → jkl, 6 → mno, 7 → pqrs, 8 → tuv, 9 → wxyz.

Given a string `digits` containing only `2`–`9`, return **all letter strings** the digits could represent (one letter per digit, in the same order). Return an empty list for an empty input. Any order is accepted.
constraints: digits[i] is a character from '2' to '9'
hints: If there were always exactly two digits, two nested loops would do. What replaces a variable number of nested loops?
Recursion: one level of recursion per digit, one loop iteration per letter of that digit.
backtrack(i): if i === digits.length record path; else for each letter of digits[i]: push, backtrack(i + 1), pop.

approaches.name: Iterative queue (BFS)
approaches.idea: Start with [""]; for each digit replace every partial string by its extensions with that digit's letters.

approaches.name: Backtracking (DFS)
approaches.idea: One recursion level per digit; at level i loop over the letters of digits[i], push, recurse, pop.

solution.summary: Backtracking with one recursion level per digit: at level i I loop over the letters of digits[i], append one, recurse to i + 1 and remove it; at i == length the path is a full combination. With k digits there are at most 4ᵏ results of length k, so O(4ᵏ·k).
solution.explanation:
This is the cleanest example of **recursion replacing a variable number of nested loops**. With two digits you would write two loops; with k digits you need k loops, and recursion gives you exactly that: each call is one loop level.

1. Handle the empty input first: return `[]`, not `[""]`.
2. `backtrack(i)`: if `i === digits.length`, every digit has a letter — push `path.join("")`.
3. Otherwise, for each letter `ch` of `keys[digits[i]]`: push `ch`, call `backtrack(i + 1)`, pop.

**Complexity:** the tree has one level per digit and each node has 3 or 4 children, so there are at most 4ᵏ leaves; building each string costs O(k). The recursion is only k deep.

Unlike Combination Sum or N-Queens nothing is ever pruned — every leaf is an answer — which is why this is often the first backtracking problem to practise.

complexity.time: O(4ᵏ·k) — up to 4 letters per digit gives at most 4ᵏ strings of length k
complexity.space: O(k) — recursion depth and path (output excluded)

keyPoints: Recursion = a variable number of nested loops (one level per digit)
Return [] for empty input, not [""]
Answer count is the product of letters per digit, at most 4ᵏ
Mention the iterative queue version as an alternative

Choose 'd' for digit '3', recurse with i = 1. Digit '4' maps to "ghi": 3 more branches.
Choose 'g': i = 2 = digits.length, so every digit has a letter → record **dg**, then pop it.
Choose 'h': i = 2 = digits.length, so every digit has a letter → record **dh**, then pop it.
Choose 'i': i = 2 = digits.length, so every digit has a letter → record **di**, then pop it.
Back at the root: pop 'd', then choose 'e' and run the same loop over "ghi": record **eg**, **eh**, **ei**. Shown right after recording ei (path = [e, i]).
Back at the root: pop 'e', then choose 'f': record **fg**, **fh**, **fi**. Shown right after recording fi (path = [f, i]).
Done: 3 × 3 = **9** combinations — one per leaf. In general the answer has up to 4ᵏ strings for k digits (7 and 9 have four letters).

visuals.caption: Breadth-first: each digit extends every partial string in the queue. Blue = just enqueued.

steps.note: The same answer **iteratively** (BFS): start the queue with one empty combination.
Digit '3' ("def"): dequeue "" and enqueue it extended by each letter: d, e, f.
Digit '4' ("ghi"): dequeue "d" and enqueue it extended by each letter: dg, dh, di.
Digit '4' ("ghi"): dequeue "e" and enqueue it extended by each letter: eg, eh, ei.
Digit '4' ("ghi"): dequeue "f" and enqueue it extended by each letter: fg, fh, fi.
Every digit processed: the queue holds all 9 combinations. Same O(4ᵏ·k) work as the recursion, but it keeps a whole level in memory at once.

pitfalls: Returning [""] for an empty input
Forgetting that 7 and 9 have four letters (hard-coding 3)
Using string concatenation in a loop and also popping — pick one style (immutable string argument or shared array with pop)

followUps.question: How would you return only combinations that are real words?
followUps.answer: Load the dictionary into a trie and prune: at each level only follow letters that keep the prefix inside the trie. Whole subtrees disappear early.

followUps.question: What if the digits string were very long?
followUps.answer: The output itself is exponential (4ᵏ), so no algorithm can list it fast. Return a lazy iterator/generator, or count the combinations instead (product of letter counts).

questions.title: N-Queens
questions.prompt:
Place `n` queens on an `n × n` chessboard so that **no two queens attack each other** — no two share a row, a column or a diagonal.

Return **every** distinct arrangement. Describe each board as a list of `n` strings where `Q` is a queen and `.` an empty square (row 0 first). Any order of boards is accepted.

examples.explanation: Exactly two solutions, mirror images of each other
No arrangement works for n = 2 or n = 3

hints: Two queens can never share a row, so exactly one queen goes in each row. What do you choose for row r?
Fill rows top to bottom; for row r try every column that is not attacked, recurse to row r + 1, then remove the queen.
Make the "is it attacked?" test O(1): keep sets of used columns, used r − c values (one per "\" diagonal) and used r + c values (one per "/" diagonal).

approaches.name: Try every placement
approaches.idea: Choose n of the n² squares and check each set: C(n², n) candidates — about 1.8 × 10³ for n = 4 but 4.4 × 10⁹ for n = 8.

approaches.name: One queen per row, scan the board
approaches.idea: Backtrack row by row; check a square by scanning the earlier rows for conflicts.

approaches.name: Backtracking with column / diagonal sets
approaches.idea: Same search, but cols, r − c and r + c sets make each safety check O(1).
approaches.time: O(n!) — the first row has n options, the next at most n − 1, …
approaches.space: O(n) for the sets and recursion (plus output)

solution.summary: Backtracking row by row: each row gets exactly one queen, so for row r I try every column that is not in the used-columns set, the r − c diagonal set or the r + c anti-diagonal set; place it, recurse to r + 1, then remove it. When r reaches n I record the board. The search is bounded by n!.
solution.explanation:
**Reduce the search space first:** two queens in the same row attack each other, so every row has exactly one queen. The decision at level r is just *which column*.

### Constant-time conflict checks
- Same **column**: keep a set `cols`.
- Same **"\" diagonal**: r − c is constant along it → set `diag`.
- Same **"/" anti-diagonal**: r + c is constant along it → set `anti`.

### Algorithm
1. `place(r)`: if `r === n`, all rows are filled → convert `queens` to strings and record.
2. For each column `c`: skip it if `c`, `r − c` or `r + c` is already used.
3. Otherwise **choose** (add to `queens` and the three sets), **explore** `place(r + 1)`, **un-choose** (remove from all four).

**Pruning is what makes it fast:** a wrong early queen is discovered as soon as some later row has no safe column, and the whole subtree below it is skipped. For n = 8 the search visits a few thousand nodes instead of billions of placements.

**Counts to remember:** n = 1 → 1, n = 2 and 3 → 0, n = 4 → 2, n = 8 → 92.

code.code:
def solve_n_queens(n: int) -> list[list[str]]:
    result, queens = [], []  # queens[r] = column of the queen in row r
    cols, diag, anti = set(), set(), set()

    def place(r: int) -> None:
        if r == n:
            result.append(['.' * c + 'Q' + '.' * (n - c - 1) for c in queens])
            return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or r - c in diag or r + c in anti:
                continue  # attacked
            queens.append(c)  # place the queen and block its column and diagonals
            cols.add(c)
            diag.add(r - c)
            anti.add(r + c)
            place(r + 1)  # fill the next row
            queens.pop()  # remove it again (backtrack)
            cols.remove(c)
            diag.remove(r - c)
            anti.remove(r + c)

    place(0)
    return result

complexity.time: O(n!) — row r has at most n − r safe columns; building each board costs O(n²)
complexity.space: O(n) — queens array, three sets and recursion depth n (output excluded)

keyPoints: One queen per row turns the problem into choosing a column per row
cols, r − c and r + c sets give O(1) conflict checks
Choose → explore → un-choose: remove the queen from every set on the way back
Pruning cuts subtrees early; worst case is bounded by n!
Know the small counts (4 → 2, 8 → 92) to sanity-check

Row 1: col 0 (same column), col 1 (diagonal r−c = 0) are attacked; col 2 is safe → place a queen at (1, 2) and add 2, -1, 3 to cols / diag / anti. × marks squares it now attacks.
Row 2: every column is attacked — col 0 (same column), col 1 (anti-diagonal r+c = 3), col 2 (same column), col 3 (diagonal r−c = -1). **Dead end**: return to row 1.
Remove the queen at (1, 2). Row 1: col 3 is safe → place a queen at (1, 3) and add 3, -2, 4 to cols / diag / anti. × marks squares it now attacks.
Row 2: col 0 (same column) is attacked; col 1 is safe → place a queen at (2, 1) and add 1, 1, 3 to cols / diag / anti. × marks squares it now attacks.
Row 3: every column is attacked — col 0 (same column), col 1 (same column), col 2 (diagonal r−c = 1), col 3 (same column). **Dead end**: return to row 2.

Remove the queen at (2, 1). Row 2: col 2 (diagonal r−c = 0), col 3 (same column) are attacked and no columns are left → return. Remove the queen at (1, 3). Row 1 has no columns left → return. Remove the queen at (0, 0). Row 0: col 1 is safe → place a queen at (0, 1) and add 1, -1, 1 to cols / diag / anti. × marks squares it now attacks.

Row 1: col 0 (anti-diagonal r+c = 1), col 1 (same column), col 2 (diagonal r−c = -1) are attacked; col 3 is safe → place a queen at (1, 3) and add 3, -2, 4 to cols / diag / anti. × marks squares it now attacks.
Row 2: col 0 is safe → place a queen at (2, 0) and add 0, 2, 2 to cols / diag / anti. × marks squares it now attacks.
Row 3: col 0 (same column), col 1 (same column) are attacked; col 2 is safe → place a queen at (3, 2) and add 2, 1, 5 to cols / diag / anti. × marks squares it now attacks.
All 4 rows have a queen (r === n) → record the board. queens = [1, 3, 0, 2] means row r has its queen in column queens[r].
Letting the search run on finds one more board, queens = [2, 0, 3, 1] (the mirror image). For n = 4 the result has **2** solutions; for n = 8 it has 92.

visuals.caption: Each cell shows the key the solution stores in its sets (last step: "r−c|r+c" for the candidates in row 2).

steps.note: Cell value = **r − c**. Moving down-right adds 1 to both r and c, so r − c stays the same along every "\" diagonal. The highlighted cells all have r − c = 0.
Cell value = **r + c**. Moving down-left adds 1 to r and subtracts 1 from c, so r + c is constant along every "/" anti-diagonal. Highlighted: r + c = 3.

A queen at (1, 2) attacks column 2, diagonal r − c = −1 and anti-diagonal r + c = 3. Checking a new square is three O(1) set lookups instead of scanning the board. There are 2n − 1 diagonals of each kind (Java offsets r − c by n − 1 to use an array).

Now test row 2 against the sets cols = {2}, diag = {−1}, anti = {3}: (2, 0) gives c = 0, r − c = 2, r + c = 2 — none used, so it is **safe**. (2, 1) has r + c = 3, (2, 2) shares column 2 and (2, 3) has r − c = −1, so they are attacked.

pitfalls: Checking only one diagonal direction (forgetting r + c or r − c)
Forgetting to remove the column / diagonal keys when backtracking
Using r − c directly as an array index in Java/C — it can be negative; offset it by n − 1
Scanning the whole board for every check, turning each step into O(n²)

followUps.question: How would you only count the solutions (N-Queens II)?
followUps.answer: Same backtracking but increment a counter instead of building boards. Bitmasks for cols/diagonals make it very fast: available = ~(cols | diag | anti) & ((1 << n) - 1), then iterate its set bits.

followUps.question: How is this related to Sudoku solving?
followUps.answer: Same pattern: pick an empty cell, try every digit not used in its row, column or box (three sets), recurse, undo. Choosing the cell with the fewest options first prunes even more.

questions.title: Word Search
questions.prompt: You are given an `m × n` grid of letters `board` and a string `word`. Return `true` if `word` can be spelled by a path of **adjacent** cells (up, down, left or right — not diagonal) in which every cell is used **at most once**; otherwise return `false`.

examples.explanation: N has two neighbouring E's, but neither E touches a second E
The A at (0,0) cannot be used twice

constraints: board and word contain only English letters
hints: Every cell that holds word[0] is a possible starting point. From there, what does the next letter depend on?
Use DFS: dfs(r, c, k) asks "can word[k..] be spelled starting at (r, c)?". Try all four neighbours for k + 1.
A cell must not be reused within one path: overwrite it with "#" before recursing and restore it afterwards so other paths can still use it.

approaches.name: DFS with a visited set
approaches.idea: From every start cell run DFS; keep a set of "r,c" keys on the current path and delete the key when backtracking.

approaches.name: DFS marking the board in place
approaches.idea: Same search, but temporarily overwrite the cell with "#" instead of using a set, then restore it.

solution.summary: DFS with backtracking from every cell: dfs(r, c, k) fails if (r, c) is off the board or does not hold word[k]; otherwise it marks the cell "#", tries the four neighbours for k + 1 and restores the cell before returning. Reaching k == word.length means the word was found. Time O(R·C·3^L), space O(L).
solution.explanation:
### The recursive question
`dfs(r, c, k)` = "can I spell `word[k..]` starting at cell (r, c)?"
1. If `k === word.length` → every letter matched → `true`.
2. If (r, c) is off the board or `board[r][c] !== word[k]` → `false`. A cell marked `#` never equals a letter, so this also blocks reuse.
3. **Choose:** save the letter and write `#`.
4. **Explore:** try down, up, right, left with `k + 1`; `||` stops at the first success.
5. **Un-choose:** put the letter back so other paths (from other start cells or other branches) can use it.

The outer double loop starts a DFS from every cell.

### Why un-marking matters
In the trace, the path S → E(1,0) → A(2,0) dead-ends. If (1,0) and (2,0) stayed marked, a later path that needs them would wrongly fail. This is the difference from flood fill (Number of Islands), where cells stay visited forever.

### Complexity
From each of the R·C start cells the first step has 4 directions and every later step at most 3 (you cannot go back to the cell you came from), so O(R·C·4·3^(L−1)) = O(R·C·3^L). The recursion depth is L.

### Practical pruning (good to mention)
- If the word is longer than R·C, or the board lacks enough copies of some letter, return false immediately (count letters first).
- If the last letter of the word is rarer on the board than the first, search for the reversed word — fewer start points.

questions.title: Word Search II
questions.prompt:
You are given an `m × n` board of lowercase letters and a list of distinct `words`. Return every word from the list that can be spelled by a path of **adjacent** cells (up, down, left or right, not diagonal) in which each cell is used **at most once within that word**.

Each word that can be found appears **once** in the output, in any order.

examples.explanation: cat = (0,0) → (0,1) → (1,1), car = (0,0) → (0,1) → (0,2), tea = (1,1) → (2,1) → (2,2). "tea" can also be spelled through (1,2) but is reported once. "cart" fails because no t touches the r, and "bat" fails because no a touches the b.
"aba" would need the a at (0,0) twice.

constraints: board and words contain only lowercase English letters; all words are distinct
hints: Running Word Search once per word repeats the same board walks for every word that shares a prefix. How could one walk check many words at once?
Store all words in a trie. While the DFS walks the board, walk the trie in parallel: if the trie node has no child for the next letter, no word can continue, so stop right there.

Keep the full word in the trie node where it ends. When the DFS reaches such a node, record the word and clear it so it is reported once. On the way back, delete trie leaves that no longer lead to any word.

solution.summary: Searching for each word separately repeats the same walks, so I put all the words into a **trie** and run **one backtracking DFS from every cell** that walks the board and the trie together. If the trie has no child for the next letter, no word continues and I stop immediately. When I reach a node that stores a word, I record it and clear it so it is reported once, and on the way back I delete trie leaves that no longer lead to any word. Worst case O(m · n · 3^L), but the trie cuts off most paths.
solution.explanation:
### Why a trie?
Running Word Search once per word costs O(W · m · n · 3^L), and words like `car`, `cart` and `cat` all repeat the walk over `c → a`. A **trie** merges the words by prefix, so a single DFS serves all of them: the board path so far must spell a prefix that exists in the trie.

### The search
`dfs(r, c, parent)`, where `parent` is the trie node for the letters on the path **before** (r, c):
1. `node = parent.next.get(board[r][c])`. If there is no such child, no word continues: return. A cell marked `'#'` (already on the path) is never a trie key, so this also stops a cell being reused.
2. If `node.word` is set, add it to `found` and set it to `null` so another path cannot report it again. **Keep searching**: a longer word may continue from here (car → cart).
3. **Choose:** mark the cell `'#'`. **Explore:** recurse into the 4 in-bounds neighbours with `node`. **Un-choose:** restore the letter.
4. **Prune:** if `node` now has no children and no word, delete it from `parent`. Later searches then stop one letter earlier.

The outer loops call `dfs(r, c, root)` for every cell.

### Why pruning matters
Without it, a word that was already found keeps costing search time. On a board full of `a`s with the word `aaaaaaaaaa`, every one of the 144 start cells would explore the same huge tree even after the word is found at the first cell. With pruning, the branch disappears once its words are found. In the example, once `tea` is found its `a` and `e` nodes are deleted on the way back, so the second path to `tea` (through the e at (1,2)) stops right after the `t`; then `t` itself is deleted.

### Complexity
- Building the trie: O(S), where S is the total number of letters in all words.
- Search: from each of the m · n cells, the first step has 4 directions and each later step at most 3 (you cannot step back onto the path), up to depth L = the longest word: O(m · n · 4 · 3^(L−1)) = O(m · n · 3^L) in the worst case. The trie usually prunes far more.
- Space: O(S) for the trie and O(L) for the recursion.

complexity.time: O(S + m · n · 3^L) — S letters to build the trie; each start cell explores at most 4 · 3^(L−1) paths of length ≤ L
complexity.space: O(S) — the trie, plus O(L) recursion depth

Stop as soon as the trie has no child for the next letter (prefix pruning)
Store the whole word at its end node; record it once, then clear it to avoid duplicates
Mark the cell before recursing and restore it afterwards (backtracking)
Delete trie leaves that no longer lead to a word, so finished words stop costing time
O(m · n · 3^L) worst case, O(S) space for the trie

visuals.caption: Blue = current cell, light blue = cells on the current path (temporarily "#"), red = neighbours rejected because the trie has no matching child, green = a found word / the final answer cells.

steps.note: The trie holds cat, car, cart, tea and bat. The outer loop calls `dfs(0, 0, root)`: "c" is a child of the root, so the path "c" is a real prefix. Mark (0,0) as `#` and explore its neighbours.
Down (1,0) is "b", but no word starts with "cb": the trie node for "c" has no child "b", so that call returns at once (red). Right (0,1) is "a" → prefix "ca" exists, so mark it and go deeper.
Down (1,1) is "t": the trie node for "cat" stores a word. Add **"cat"** to `found` and set `node.word = null` so no second path can report it again.
No neighbour of (1,1) continues "cat" ((1,0), (2,1), (1,2) fail, (0,1) is in use). Restore (1,1); the "cat" node now has no children and no word, so **delete it** from the trie.
Back at (0,1), try right (0,2) "r": **"car"** is a word, record it. Do not stop here: the node still has the child "t" for "cart", so the search keeps going from (0,2).
From (0,2) the only free neighbour is (1,2) "e", but "car" continues only with "t", so "cart" is not on the board. Restore (0,2) and return; the "car" node keeps its "t" child, so it is not pruned.

The frames for (0,1) and (0,0) restore their cells too. The outer loop moves on: (0,1) "a" and (0,2) "r" return immediately because no word starts with them. (1,0) "b" matches the root's child "b", so mark it and look for an "a" next to it.
The neighbours of (1,0) are (0,0) "c", (2,0) "s" and (1,1) "t", none of them "a", so "bat" is impossible. Restore (1,0); the "b" branch stays because "bat" was never found.
(1,1) "t" starts the prefix "t". Its neighbours (0,1) "a" and (1,0) "b" do not continue it, but down (2,1) "e" gives "te": mark it and continue.

From (2,1), (2,0) "s" fails and right (2,2) "a" completes **"tea"**. Record it and clear the word. When these frames return, the "tea" node and then the "te" node are empty leaves, so both get deleted.

Back at (1,1), right (1,2) "e" would spell "tea" a second time via (1,2) → (2,2). But "t" no longer has an "e" child (it was pruned), so that call stops after one lookup. Then "t" itself is empty and is deleted from the root.
The remaining cells (1,2) "e", (2,0) "s", (2,1) "e" and (2,2) "a" are not children of the root, so each returns at once. Result: **["cat", "car", "tea"]**; "cart" and "bat" are not on the board.

visuals.title: The trie shrinks as words are found
visuals.caption: ✓ = node stores a word that has not been reported yet. Light blue = trie path matching the board path, green = word just found, amber = node that survives because it still leads to a word, grey = words that are not on the board.

steps.note: Insert cat, car, cart, tea and bat. Shared prefixes are stored once: cat, car and cart all start with c → a. A ✓ marks a node that stores a whole word (`node.word`).
The board path c → a → t reaches the "cat" node, which holds a word: report it and clear `node.word` (the ✓ disappears) so it is never reported twice.
Backtracking out of "cat": the node has no children and no word, so `parent.next.delete("t")` removes it. Any later search reaching "ca" will not even try a "t".
"car" is found and cleared, but the node stays: its child "t" still leads to "cart". Only nodes with no word and no children are removed, and "cart" is never completed because no "t" touches (0,2).
The search from (1,0) "b" finds no neighbouring "a", so the trie is unchanged. Then the board path t → e → a reaches the "tea" node: report **"tea"** and clear its word.

On the way back the "tea" and "te" nodes become empty and are deleted, so the second board path to "tea" (through (1,2)) stops at its second letter; then the empty "t" is deleted from the root too. The trie that is left holds only the words not on the board: cart and bat.

pitfalls: Reporting a word twice when it can be spelled along two paths; clear node.word after recording it
Returning from the DFS as soon as a word is found, which misses longer words that extend it (car → cart)
Forgetting to restore the cell after the recursive calls, so later paths think it is still in use
Running Word Search I once per word: correct, but far too slow with thousands of words

followUps.question: Why store the whole word in the trie node instead of a boolean isEnd?
followUps.answer: The DFS can add the word to the result directly, without building the path string as it goes, and setting it to null is an O(1) way to avoid duplicates.

followUps.question: How can you cut the work before the search even starts?
followUps.answer: Count the letters on the board and skip any word that needs more copies of a letter than the board has, or that is longer than m · n. Those words can never be found, and leaving them out keeps the trie smaller.

quiz.question: What happens when a recursive function has no reachable base case?
options: It returns undefined after n calls
It keeps calling itself until the call stack overflows
The runtime converts it into a loop automatically
It runs forever without using extra memory
quiz.explanation: Every call pushes a new stack frame, so the stack eventually overflows: RangeError in JavaScript, RecursionError in Python, StackOverflowError in Java. V8, CPython and the JVM do not turn recursion into loops (no tail-call optimisation), so it will not run forever silently.

quiz.question: What is the space complexity of `factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1)` with base case n ≤ 1?
quiz.explanation: All n frames are on the call stack at the same time before the base case returns, so the recursion uses O(n) space. O(1) is the space of the loop version.

quiz.question: What does this print (one number per line)?
quiz.explanation: The first console.log runs on the way down (3, 2, 1). The second runs after the inner call returns, so frames finish in reverse order (1, 2, 3). Code after a recursive call executes while the stack unwinds.

quiz.question: How many subsets does an array of 5 distinct elements have, including the empty subset?
quiz.explanation: Each element is either in or out: 2⁵ = 32. 120 = 5! would be the number of permutations, and 10 = C(5, 2) only counts subsets of size 2.

quiz.question: How many permutations does an array of 4 distinct elements have?
quiz.explanation: 4 choices for the first position, 3 for the second, 2, then 1: 4! = 24. 16 = 2⁴ is the number of subsets.

quiz.question: In Combination Sum (each candidate may be reused), why does the recursive call pass `i` instead of `i + 1`?
options: To visit the candidates in sorted order
So the same candidate can be chosen again
To prevent both [2,3] and [3,2] from appearing
To make sure the recursion terminates
quiz.explanation: Passing i keeps the current candidate available at the next level, which allows [2,2,3]. Preventing [2,3] vs [3,2] is the job of the start index itself (never going back to smaller indices), not of i vs i + 1.

quiz.question: In the subsets solution, what goes wrong if you write `result.push(path)` instead of `result.push([...path])`?
options: Duplicate subsets appear in the result
Every entry refers to the same array, which is empty at the end
quiz.explanation: path is one shared array that keeps being pushed and popped. Storing the reference means all 2ⁿ entries point to that array, which ends empty after the last pop. A copy freezes the subset at that moment.

quiz.question: In N-Queens, which value is the same for every square on one "\" diagonal (top-left to bottom-right)?
quiz.explanation: Moving down-right increases r and c by 1, so r − c is unchanged. r + c is constant on the other ("/") diagonals, which is why the solution keeps two separate sets.

quiz.question: In Generate Parentheses, when is it legal to append ")"?
quiz.explanation: A ")" must close a bracket that is currently open, so the count of ")" may never exceed the count of "(". close < n alone would allow ")(" as a prefix.

quiz.question: Why does Word Search restore board[r][c] after exploring the neighbours?
options: To free memory used by the recursion
So that other paths can still use that cell
quiz.explanation: Marking the cell prevents reusing it on the current path (that is what stops cycles). Restoring it on the way back is the backtracking step: a different path, from another branch or start cell, may legitimately pass through it.

quiz.question: myPow(x, n) computes half = myPow(x, ⌊n/2⌋) once and squares it. What is its time complexity?
quiz.explanation: n halves on every call, so there are about log₂ n + 1 calls with O(1) work each. Calling myPow(x, n/2) twice instead of reusing half would make it O(n).

quiz.question: nums may contain duplicates, e.g. [1, 2, 2]. Which change makes the subsets backtracking avoid duplicate subsets?
options: Store the subsets in a Set of arrays
Sort nums, then skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] === nums[i − 1]
Skip nums[i] when used[i − 1] is false
Recurse with i instead of i + 1
quiz.explanation: After sorting, equal values are adjacent; skipping a repeated value at the same level (i > start) means each distinct choice starts only one branch. A Set of arrays does not work in JavaScript (arrays compare by reference), and recursing with i would allow reuse.
